reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: What the reader will learn: running a migration in three phases, counting unfinished ones, and making the case for capacity to finish them.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: The chapter's three main claims: shared debt is removed by migrations, the payoff comes only at completion, and funding plus a cap keeps delivery going.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: The three failure patterns of the book that this chapter helps avoid, each tied to migrations.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Corvane completed one release-path migration in 2024, but two years and much growth later runs many parallel systems with none retired.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The chapter's thesis that debt at scale is retired by three-phase, funded, limited migrations that must be finished / the roadmap of what the chapter covers and how it fits the part.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: How the 2024 release-path move went from diagnosis through a pilot on a hard team to all eleven teams moved and the old form closed.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: As Corvane grew, new teams brought extra deploy methods, brokers and an identity library with nobody responsible for consolidating, until the 2026 strategy assigned a rule and an owner.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The measurable cost of the unconsolidated state in 2026: higher failure rates for newer teams, a stretched platform team, and a broker count about to rise.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Shared Debt Needs a Migration ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Technical debt splits into local debt a team can repay itself and shared debt that no single team's backlog can reach.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Shared Debt Needs a Migration ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Larson's argument that growth keeps outdating tools, so migrations are usually the only route to real progress on debt.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Shared Debt Needs a Migration ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The book's definition of a migration as moving all users until the old way is switched off, and its nature as a trade of output now for capacity later.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why a Half-Finished Migration Is Worse Than None ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Benefits arrive only at switch-off, since the organization runs one system before, two during and one after.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why a Half-Finished Migration Is Worse Than None ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A migration that stalls midway has added debt, as two sources describe, and Corvane's uncoordinated spread is that same in-between state.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why a Half-Finished Migration Is Worse Than None ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The ability to finish migrations determines how quickly an organization can put changed decisions into effect, with pointers to related topics.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Derisk, Enable, Finish ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces Larson's three-phase playbook as the way to run a migration so it reaches its end, with its users and measure.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Derisk, Enable, Finish ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Derisk phase: test the new way first on the hardest, least typical teams, as Corvane's pilot did.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Derisk, Enable, Finish ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Enable phase: build tooling and support that make moving cheap, incremental and reversible for the remaining teams.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Derisk, Enable, Finish ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Finish phase: block new use of the old way, chase the remaining teams, move the last ones yourself and retire the old system; Corvane did this in 2024 but did not keep new teams on the path.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Derisk, Enable, Finish ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Each migration needs a single owner accountable for completion and switch-off rather than for the launch.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Reserve Capacity and Limit Migrations in Flight ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A migration costs both the owning team and the moving teams, and the moving teams' larger cost should be counted up front.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Reserve Capacity and Limit Migrations in Flight ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The moving teams' cost should be funded by a fixed share of capacity set aside in planning, as Corvane did for one team and then for all.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Reserve Capacity and Limit Migrations in Flight ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Capping concurrent migrations, with three sequencing rules, keeps the reserved share from being spread too thin and keeps delivery predictable.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Count the Unfinished, Then Finish, Reverse or Wait ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Find the real number of open migrations by listing every system meant to go, with its teams, owner and end date.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Count the Unfinished, Then Finish, Reverse or Wait ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Diagnose each stalled migration by which of the three phases it skipped, judged from its visible symptoms.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Count the Unfinished, Then Finish, Reverse or Wait ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Every open migration must receive an explicit decision to complete, undo or defer it; undoing counts as a valid ending.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Anti-Patterns: The Graveyard, the Clean-Up Sprint and the Announcement ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Three typical ways migrations fail, each missing something the patterns provide and linked to a named failure pattern.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane Counts Its Migrations ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: At the end of 2026 Corvane's leaders make the inventory of systems to be retired with teams, owners and dates.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane Counts Its Migrations ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: What the inventory revealed: few rows owned and dated, one overloaded owner, one stalled move and one move by announcement only.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane Counts Its Migrations ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The resulting 2027 plan: the order of the moves, which is finished, reversed or deferred, who owns each, and where the capacity comes from.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane Counts Its Migrations ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The costs the plan carries for moving teams and for systems kept running, and a note that no outcomes are claimed.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What AI Changes Here ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Coding agents are starting to take over the mechanical bulk of migrations, supported by a Google experience report that is suggestive but not conclusive.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What AI Changes Here ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A conjecture that agents shorten only the enabling phase while derisking and owned finishing remain, and that cheaper change may multiply systems needing retirement.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Part IV as One Loop ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The five elements of the engineering model form a cycle in which migration carries a changed policy into the landscape.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Part IV as One Loop ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Corvane's four deploy methods read as that cycle with pieces absent: no policy, no usable default path and unfinished moves.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The points the chapter takes directly from its sources.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The choices that vary with an organization's circumstances: reserve size, concurrency cap, and finish versus reverse.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The parts of the chapter that are the author's own contribution rather than the sources'.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checklist ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A restatement that everything serves retiring the old system, followed by eight practical checks for the reader's own landscape.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checklist ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Why Corvane's 2024 move ended and the later ones did not / the engineering model is now complete beside the product model, which leads into the next part on leadership structure.

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 36 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01 to p36); the three callouts match no paragraph by house format.

Two units were marked two_ideas. Introduction ¶2 holds thesis and roadmap, which the spec joins in p02 by design. Checklist ¶2 holds the Corvane callback and the hand-off, which the spec joins in p36's controlling idea. Neither is a failure.

Every unit serves the supporting claim(s) its section declares (S1 to S5); the two pointers at the end of the p11 unit (reorganizations, Building Evolutionary Architectures) are prescribed by the spec and stay subordinate.

Each table and figure is introduced or followed by a sentence saying what it shows (states table: 'The middle column is the expensive one'; diagnosis and decision tables summarized in the prose before them; count table read in the next paragraph; both figures captioned and discussed). Quotations are attributed and framed; the Google report is qualified as an experience report.

Larson's concepts name An Elegant Puzzle and the concept; the order-of-magnitude figure is given as 'his rule of thumb'; Fournier and Nowland are named with Platform Engineering; every extension is marked (my wording, my arrangement, my reading, the part I add, my way, my extension, my recommendation, is mine).

results.draft_locus: Why a Half-Finished Migration Is Worse Than None ¶3
results.quote: Finishing also matters beyond any one migration.
results.finding: The spec declares cause_effect carrying over 'a stalled migration as added debt'. The boundary sentence expresses addition ('also') and does not pick up the stalled migration or added debt; the consequence only appears three sentences later ('So an organization's ability...').
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, decision 'waive by rule' under the rule 'max two rounds per chapter': this finding remained after the last check round allowed. It was listed in the writer's report to the author; where the writer revised the unit afterwards, the revision was not re-checked by fresh readers, and where the writer left the unit unchanged, the finding stands as written.

results.finding: All other declared transitions (33 boundaries) express the declared relationship and pick up the declared known information at the boundary, e.g. 'Then Corvane grew.', 'If the finish decides the return...', 'Phases and an owner still need capacity', 'A limit presumes that you know how many migrations are in flight', 'With the phase known'.

Both flow readers named the ordering principle the spec declares (problem-solution around one case, with a dependency chain through the three patterns) and said why each section comes where it does; neither wanted the sections reordered. No point was reported by both readers and rated (a) by both, so no finding below is corroborated.

results.quote: Since 2024 not one of the older ways had been switched off.
results.finding: Reader A (3.1, rated a) could not tell which deploying ways are 'the older ways', since the ways meant to go are newer than the release path that stays; it was settled only by the worked-example table. Reader B (3.14) reported the related old/new role reversal at the 'middle column' sentence but rated it (b). Not corroborated at (a). The wording comes from the spec's hook and p04.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶2 to ¶3
results.quote: That changed in the middle of 2026, when Corvane wrote its first engineering strategy, with a rule of one standard per shared area, and made the platform team the owner of the move to the release path.
results.finding: Reader A (3.3, rated b) re-read both paragraphs to put the events in order: ¶2 ends in mid-2026 and ¶3 returns to 'this open state' and the first half of 2026. Reader B (3.6, rated b) also re-read this sentence, because 'That' covers three areas and the change covers deploying only. The section is declared chronological but p04's controlling idea ends in mid-2026 before p05's first-half figures.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶3
results.quote: By the end of the year seven of the nineteen had moved to the release path, and twelve still released in the three other ways.
results.finding: Reader B (3.1, rated a): the sentence jumps from the first half to the end of 2026 without a marker, sits between the platform-team sentence and messaging, and had to be revisited from the worked-example table to confirm the twelve teams are the same twelve. Reader A reported only the time order of the two paragraphs (b). One reader at (a).

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶3
results.quote: which meant four brokers, the three older ones and the new one, until the oldest was switched off
results.finding: Both readers stopped on the broker count (A 3.13, B 3.5, both rated b): the introduction and ¶2 say three brokers for 2026 and four first appears here; each checked which brokers are in which row of the count table. Resolved by re-reading.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene: One Migration Finished, Three Areas Left Open ¶2
results.quote: The new teams brought three other ways of deploying, mostly scripts copied or written in a team's first weeks.
results.finding: Reader B (3.2, rated a) went back from the count table to the scene: the group pipeline, a move one product group began on purpose, arrives in the table as new information and does not fit 'scripts' or 'nobody had the job'. Reader A (3.14, rated b) re-read to hold the group pipeline's two roles (system to be switched off, and target of a reversed migration). Same object, not both (a).

results.quote: The user of this rule is the executive who sponsors a migration. Its outcome measure is that every open migration has a named owner and an end date.
results.finding: Both readers (A 3.7, B 3.10, both rated b) looked back to see why one pattern section carries two users and two measures, the first pair arriving before the pattern is described. The spec prescribes a user and measure in both p12 and p16.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Reserve Capacity and Limit Migrations in Flight ¶2
results.quote: Corvane did this for one team in 2024, when the Identity team, halfway through replacing its permission model, got two more quarters without new roadmap commitments.
results.finding: Both readers (A 3.9, B 3.11, both rated b) re-read to see how this is an example of the reserved share: the paragraph is about the moving teams' bill, and the Identity team here is doing its own replacement, not being moved. The example is prescribed by p18's evidence. (The Identity team itself is known to the book's reader from Corvane's story, so this is not a known_before_new failure.)

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Reserve Capacity and Limit Migrations in Flight ¶3
results.quote: A security fault can force a move outside the limit.
results.finding: Both readers (A 3.11, B 3.8, both rated b) found the exception out of place: it stands between the sentence on delivery continuing and the users and measures, connected to neither. It belongs directly after the three rules.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Count the Unfinished, Then Finish, Reverse or Wait ¶1
results.quote: Each such system is one open migration, whether or not anyone called it a project.
results.finding: Both readers (A 3.12, B 3.9, both rated b) were unsure for a moment how an 'open' migration relates to a migration 'in flight' (defined one paragraph earlier as asking teams to move now) and whether a stalled one counts against the limit; the two terms are never set side by side and only the Wait row settles it.

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: Corvane Counts Its Migrations ¶2
results.quote: Two rows of six, both in messaging, had an owner and an end date. The platform team of eight engineers was the owner in five rows, so one owner was being asked to finish five moves at once.
results.finding: Reader B (3.3, rated a) had to return to the table and count: 'owned and dated' (two rows) and 'owned by the platform team' (five rows) read as in tension at first, and 'five moves' counts the two-broker row as one move though those brokers later wait. One reader only.

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: Corvane Counts Its Migrations ¶3
results.quote: The platform team finishes one migration before it starts the next, and no product team is moved twice in one quarter.
results.finding: Reader B (3.4, rated a) was left unsure whether the rules constrain this plan: the text does not say that the identity move runs alongside because it has a different owner, nor whether any team sits on two rows of the table. One reader only.

results.quote: The claim would be confirmed if organizations that use agents for migrations report shorter enable phases while the number of systems waiting to be switched off does not fall.
results.finding: Both readers (A 3.16, B 3.12, both rated b) first lost what 'The claim' refers to, because two sentences on Corvane in 2027 and 2028 stand between the Speculative statement and its confirmation test.

results.quote: The migration is the last of the five parts of the engineering model that this part of the book has built, and with it the five close into one loop.
results.finding: Both readers (A 3.17, B 3.13, both rated b) re-read because 'parts' (of the model) and 'this part' (of the book) are used in two senses in one sentence.

results.quote: all eleven teams were on it and the old request form was closed
results.finding: 'the old request form' is used before anything says that releases were requested by form; it is explained only in the next section ('the launch-request form'). Flow reader A reported it (3.2, rated a, minor); reader B did not, so it is not corroborated.

Every term on does_not_know is given before or where it is first relied on: technical debt, local and shared debt, migration against data migration, switched off, derisk/enable/finish, stopping the bleeding, migrations in flight, the four team states, operation share, paved path, message broker and identity library; lead time, change failure rate and policy are glossed too. 'Mandate' is recalled only as the end of the range 'from advice to a mandate', which the audience has from chapter 14.
The introduction opens on a specific puzzling case and states a disputable claim; none of the weak patterns applies.
The conclusion sorts what holds by how settled it is, adds a synthesis and a course of action, and hands off; it does not open with 'in conclusion', add a subtopic or end on a rephrased thesis.

Checklist ¶1 states what no single section states (the five means serve one end, the old system switched off, which also closes the loop of Part IV) and why it matters (a changed policy reaches the landscape only through a finished migration); the checks turn the so-what into action.
Part IV is synthesized as one loop in its own section and recalled in the conclusion's synthesis list, the sentence before the checklist, the eighth check and the closing paragraph.
The closing paragraph returns to Corvane's 2024 move and the later ones and says why the first ended and the others did not, as callback.how requires.
The intro reader predicted all ten sections in roadmap order, the kind of evidence (the Corvane case, Larson, reasoning from costs, a worked count) and the plain prescriptive tone.

The cold reader named the skipped finish phase (nobody accountable for the last team and the switch-off), called the two-system state added debt, and proposed finish (owner moves the rest, switch-off date) or reverse, with waiting only under the limit; this matches the expected answer.

Each of the three patterns names its user and an outcome measure: the teams that move / old system off by the planned date (plus the sponsoring executive / every open migration has an owner and end date); product teams and directors / migrations in flight and share spent; the VP Engineering or planning director / systems still waiting to be switched off per quarter.
